A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable, including v1 Appendices A–B and v2 Appendices A–C. Shared authors, the retained WSAE objective, and matching experiments establish the same research work despite substantial changes to its title and theoretical framing.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic experiments, Pythia-160M auto-interpretability results in Table 1, and ImageNet-100/ResNet-18 results in Figure 3.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds synthetic reconstruction analyses, Llama-3-8B evaluations, grouped Top-k experiments, and sensitivity analyses in Section 5 and Appendix C.1.

M1.justification: The central diagonal reweighting objective and variance/semantic-consistency weighting rules are retained. Appendix C.1 adds an evaluated activation variant that selects Top-1 separately within k groups, changing the selection procedure from global Top-k.

E1.justification: Coverage remains synthetic feature recovery, language-model feature interpretation, and ImageNet-100 vision representations. Llama and activation/proxy variants change configurations within these tasks. OpenWebText is newly disclosed as evaluation data, without establishing that the underlying corpus changed.

E2.justification: V1's synthetic comparison among no activation, JumpReLU, and Top-k in Figure 2(b) is removed. The real-data comparisons retain original SAE versus weighted SAE; newly cited architectures are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: V2 specifies fixed ReLU synthetic SAEs with 200 latent dimensions and adds ground-truth, nonzero-coordinate, and observed-feature reconstruction measurements. Additional configurations include Llama-3-8B layers and grouped Top-k. Appendix C.4 specifies correlation-based autointerpretation, conflicting with the retained main-text accuracy metric; this does not establish that existing results were recomputed.

E4.justification: New analyses distinguish ground-truth from observed-feature reconstruction, examine nonzero coordinates, vary the weighting exponent and monosemanticity proxy, and assess reconstruction tradeoffs (Figures 3 and 5). V1's activation-function and latent-width sweeps are removed, while its input-sparsity analysis is retained.

E5.justification: Neither version documents repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The added experiments do not introduce an uncertainty-reporting procedure; per-dimensional variance is a monosemanticity metric rather than run-to-run uncertainty.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the vision scores 40.2, 40.7, and 42.2 remain unchanged. V2 adds synthetic reconstruction curves, sensitivity results, grouped Top-k scores, and Llama results, while removing activation/width-sweep results. These are new experimental entries, not improvements over matching v1 settings. Table 3 inconsistently reports 67.0 versus 80.2 at layer 16 but lists a gain of 2.8.

T1.justification: V2 adds a general-sparsity closed-form optimality theorem under digon/polygon geometry, formalizes recovery up to permutation and zero padding, and expands proofs and hierarchical/attention derivations. Extreme-sparsity results receive revised statements, while the necessity-counterexample argument is replaced by shrinking/vanishing examples. Loss-gap theorems now specialize the retained decompositions to Wm = Wp^T.

C1.justification: V1 foregrounds three necessary and sufficient identifiability conditions. V2 instead foregrounds a closed-form theoretical framework and general recovery failures through feature shrinking and vanishing. Its conclusion additionally claims that increasing SAE sparsity or width cannot eliminate intrinsic interference under realistic feature sparsity. The claim that reweighting improves interpretability is retained.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations of interference-induced magnitude and importance-ranking distortions, interprets SAE features as approximate projections, and discusses reconstruction tradeoffs, feature absorption, hierarchical features, and attention extensions. It removes v1's explicit limitation that downstream applications of the recovered features remain untested.

D1.justification: Appendix C.4 adds a detailed autointerpretation procedure: 50,000 OpenWebText fragments, 64-token lengths, activation rescaling, GPT-4/GPT-3.5 roles, fragment selection, scoring, and exclusion rules. Settings for new experiments are also documented. Hardware and runtimes are retained, and the average-activated-features procedure is relocated rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: Most related-work discussion is retained, but v2 adds references including BatchTopK, Matryoshka SAEs, SAEBench, and multimodal SAEs, while removing several generic identifiability references. Appendix B newly positions the results as a nonlinear extension of sparse dictionary identifiability and connects interference to dictionary coherence.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contributions, theoretical narrative, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Mathematical preliminaries become a separate section, theoretical results are reorganized around general failure and sparse recovery, and appendices are restructured to accommodate discussion and experimental details.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn, Figure 2 is reduced from three panels to a wrapped single-panel plot, and new four-panel reconstruction and three-panel sensitivity figures are added alongside Tables 2–3. The original vision plot is retained as Figure 4. Conference formatting also changes headers, typography, and page layout.

improvement.justification: Direct ground-truth reconstruction tests, robustness analyses, and permutation-aware recovery definitions strengthen v2. However, its new central optimality proof uses an unjustified transition from the loss gradient to mean residual in Appendix A.1, Equations 17–18. The conflicting autointerpretation metrics and Table 3's inconsistent gain further weaken the added evidence. These substantive benefits and reliability problems prevent a confident net quality judgment.
